title: How do we write 36/60 in lowest terms, in steps and in one go?
description: Thirty six sixtieths is divided by two, by two again and then by three to reach three fifths. The same result comes in one go by dividing by twelve, while Keeko doubts it by stopping at nine fifteenths.
teaching_notes: One idea: dividing the top and the bottom by a common factor again and again reaches lowest terms, and the biggest common factor does it in one go. Watch for students who stop at nine fifteenths because nine is odd.

source: Express 36/60 in lowest terms, first in steps and then in one go.
video_script.why: The child reduces thirty six sixtieths to lowest terms in small steps and then in one go with the biggest common factor.
video_script.substitution: none: the book's own fraction thirty six sixtieths
video_script.anchor: the fraction thirty six sixtieths written large on the board
video_script.wrong_answer: nine fifteenths is in lowest terms
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says nine fifteenths is in lowest terms, because nine is odd and cannot be halved. But three still divides both nine and fifteen, so one more division is needed.
video_script.payoff_line: Thirty six sixtieths is three fifths in lowest terms

final_answer.spoken: thirty six sixtieths is three fifths in lowest terms

video_script.fraction_reading: thirty six sixtieths, eighteen thirtieths, nine fifteenths, three fifths
maths_rules: 36 and 60 are even: divide by 2 to get 18/30
18 and 30 are even: divide by 2 to get 9/15
9 and 15 are multiples of 3: divide by 3 to get 3/5; 3 and 5 share only 1
in one go: 36 = 3 × 12 and 60 = 5 × 12, so dividing by 12 gives 3/5
slip: Keeko stops at 9/15 because 9 is odd, but 3 still divides both 9 and 15
video_script.design: One idea: keep dividing by a common factor until none is left, or divide once by the biggest one. The fraction changes down a column on the board.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: both even, divide by 2: 36/60 gives 18/30
narration: <bookmark mark='even'/>Step one, thirty six and sixty are both even, so divide the top and the bottom by two.
<bookmark mark='half'/>We get eighteen thirtieths.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: both even again, divide by 2: 18/30 gives 9/15
narration: <bookmark mark='even'/>Step two, eighteen and thirty are both even again, so divide by two once more.
<bookmark mark='half'/>We get nine fifteenths.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: both multiples of 3, divide by 3: 9/15 gives 3/5; 3 and 5 share only 1

narration: <bookmark mark='three'/>Step three, nine and fifteen are both multiples of three, so divide by three.
<bookmark mark='third'/>We get three fifths.
<bookmark mark='only'/>Three and five share no factor except one, so we can stop.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: in one go: 36 = 3 × 12 and 60 = 5 × 12, so divide both by 12: (36 ÷ 12)/(60 ÷ 12)

marks.twelve: 36 is split into 3 × 12 and 60 into 5 × 12 with the shared 12 circled
marks.once: an arrow marked ÷ 12 joins 36/60 straight to 3/5

narration: <bookmark mark='twelve'/>Step four, in one go. Thirty six is three times twelve, and sixty is five times twelve.
<bookmark mark='once'/>Dividing both by twelve gives three fifths at once.

narration: <bookmark mark='pay'/>Thirty six sixtieths is three fifths in lowest terms.
Both ways reach the same answer.
<bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks nine fifteenths is in lowest terms, because nine is odd and cannot be halved.
<bookmark mark='three'/>But three still divides both nine and fifteen.
<bookmark mark='rule'/>Odd numbers can share factors too, so one more division is needed.
